mcqs.question: Why is `Option<T> = Some(T) | None` classified as a sum type rather than a product type?
options: Because a value is exactly one of the two alternatives (Some or None), never both, unlike a product type where all fields are present simultaneously
Because Option<T> can hold multiple values of type T at once
Because None always carries a default value of type T internally
Because Some and None must both be present in every Option<T> value
mcqs.explanation: The defining sum-type property is exclusivity — exactly one alternative holds at a time — which is exactly Some-or-None, never both; a product type instead requires all its fields present together. Option<T> holds at most one T (never multiple), None carries no value at all (not a default), and the two alternatives are never simultaneously present.

mcqs.question: How does a `Result<T, E>` value tagged as `Ok` differ structurally from one tagged as `Err`?
options: Both tags always carry both a T and an E value, differing only in which one is considered active
There is no structural difference; the tag is purely cosmetic and unused at runtime
An Ok value contains only its T payload with no E-shaped slot, and an Err value contains only its E payload with no T-shaped slot — the shape itself depends on the tag
Err always contains a T value that gets discarded
mcqs.explanation: A sum type's tagged value genuinely only carries the payload for its active alternative — there's no unused slot for the other case sitting around, unlike a product type with an optional/unused field. The tag is functionally load-bearing, not cosmetic, and neither variant secretly carries the other's payload type.

mcqs.question: A new variant `Triangle` is added to the `Shape` sum type, but the `area` function's match expression isn't updated. What happens?
options: The program compiles and area() silently returns 0 for any Triangle
Nothing changes, since match expressions always have an implicit default case
The compiler rejects the program as a non-exhaustive match, because Shape's closed set of alternatives lets it verify every case is handled
The program compiles, but throws a runtime exception only when a Triangle is actually matched
mcqs.explanation: Exhaustiveness checking is exactly this: because the sum type's alternatives form a closed, complete set, the compiler can verify at compile time that every alternative is handled, catching the missing Triangle case before the program ever runs. There's no silent compilation, no implicit default in an exhaustively-checked match, and no need to wait for a runtime occurrence to discover the gap.

mcqs.question: A `RequestState` class has `isLoading`, `data`, and `error` fields that are only meant to appear in certain combinations. What does remodeling it as a sum type (`Loading | Success(data) | Failure(error)`) actually guarantee that the flag-based version doesn't?
options: It guarantees the code runs faster than the flag-based version
It guarantees every consumer will automatically derive the same interpretation without any code changes
It guarantees data and error will always be non-null simultaneously

It guarantees the nonsensical combinations (e.g. isLoading true with both data and error populated) have no constructor that could produce them — the illegal state becomes unrepresentable, not just discouraged
mcqs.explanation: The sum type's real guarantee is structural: there is no value of the new type that represents the nonsensical combination, because each alternative only carries the data relevant to it — a stronger guarantee than a convention or runtime check. It makes no performance claim, existing consumer code still needs updating to pattern-match (it doesn't automatically adapt), and it's the opposite of guaranteeing data and error are both populated — the whole point is they can never both be present.

mcqs.question: Two functions consuming the same flag-based `RequestState` struct derive "which state is this" using different field-checking orders, and disagree on a state produced by a bug. What does this scenario illustrate?
options: That flag/field combinations meant to be mutually exclusive but not enforced by the type let different consumers derive inconsistent interpretations, with no compiler error surfacing the disagreement
That sum types are strictly worse than flag-based structs for representing state
That the bug is unrelated to how RequestState's type is modeled
That this disagreement could only happen with more than three boolean flags
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the anti-pattern's cost: without the type enforcing exclusivity, different code paths can silently derive different interpretations of the same malformed value, and nothing in the type system flags it. The scenario is a direct argument for sum types over flag structs, not against them, the bug is a direct consequence of how the type is modeled, and this can happen with any number of flags including as few as two.
